6,050 m·Camp 1

Start with what touches skin.

At 6,050 metres you sweat on the fixed lines and freeze at the anchors. Merino handles both, and it still smells like nothing after a week on the mountain.

6,700 m·Camp 2

Three layers. One job each.

Camp 2 sits above House’s Chimney at 6,700 metres. The weather turns in minutes, so the system has to adjust as fast as it does: add the mid layer on the ledge, take it off for the chimney.

Mid layer

Grid Fleece Hoody

Active insulation that dumps heat on the climb and holds it on the belay.

7,350 m·Camp 3

The outer wall.

Camp 3 sits on the Black Pyramid, 7,350 metres up, where the wind decides your day. The Summit Shell 3L is the piece we tested hardest: three layers, every seam taped, a hood cut around a helmet.

7,900 m·Camp 4

Nights on the Shoulder.

Camp 4 is the last tent before the summit push, at 7,900 metres. You leave it at midnight, at −30 °C, and the only thing between you and the cold is 850-fill down in box-wall baffles.

8000 Down Suit

One piece, box-wall baffles, built for the nights above Camp 4.

8,200 m·Bottleneck

Through the Bottleneck.

The steepest, most exposed couloir on the route, under a hanging serac, at 8,200 metres. Hands on the rope, spindrift at the ankles. Two small pieces matter more here than anywhere.

Down-filled, waterproof, and dextrous enough for an ascender.
